title: Unit 2c - Dynamic Memory Allocation
summary: Title slide introducing the Dynamic Memory Allocation unit for CS103, taught by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: This is the title slide for Unit 2c covering Dynamic Memory Allocation in CS 103. The unit explores how programs can allocate and manage memory at runtime using C++ mechanisms such as new and delete. Topics include motivations for dynamic allocation, heap memory, pointer usage patterns, and common pitfalls like memory leaks and dangling pointers.
notes_text: This unit is a foundational topic in C++ programming. Understanding dynamic memory allocation is essential for building data structures, managing resources, and writing robust programs that handle variable-sized data.

title: One or Many - Pointer Ambiguity
summary: Explains that C/C++ pointers do not distinguish between pointing to a single variable or an array, requiring context and documentation to clarify usage.
main_text: A strange question is posed: Is 3240 McClintock Ave. the address of a single-family house or a large dormitory with many suites? We cannot know just from the address. In the same way, C/C++ does not differentiate whether a pointer points to a single variable or an array. An int* may point to 1 int or an array of ints. It can only be determined based on how the context of the code that uses it. Good commenting and documentation should describe this. Two code examples illustrate the ambiguity. In the first, a function void f1(int* p) decrements the integer pointed to by p using *p -= 1, treating p as a pointer to a single variable. In the second, the same function signature void f1(int* p) uses a loop for(int i=0; i < 10; i++) { p[i] = 0; } to set array elements to zero, treating p as a pointer to an array.
notes_text: This is a critical concept for understanding pointer-based programming. The type system alone cannot tell you whether a pointer references one element or many. Always document whether a pointer parameter expects a single value or an array to prevent bugs and improve code readability.

title: Reasons To Use Pointers
summary: Presents three reasons to use pointers: pass-by-reference, dynamic memory allocation, and accessing specific hardware locations.
main_text: There are three key reasons to use pointers in C/C++. Reason 1: Use pointers when you need pass-by-reference (as opposed to pass-by-value), either to change a variable (or variables) local to one function in some other function (analogy: a Google-doc link with 'Can Edit' permission), or to avoid making needless copies of data which wastes time (analogy: a Google-doc link with 'Can View' permission, think large arrays). Reason 2: Use pointers when you perform dynamic memory allocation. Reason 3: We need to access a specific hardware location in the computer. This is not covered in this class but in EE 109/CS 356. It is useful for embedded systems and device programming. All of these will be explained in the following slides.
notes_text: Pass-by-reference is the most commonly encountered reason in introductory courses. Dynamic memory allocation becomes critical when building data structures like linked lists, trees, and when array sizes are not known at compile time. Hardware access is an advanced use case relevant to systems programming.

title: Dynamic Memory Allocation - Section Divider
summary: Section divider slide introducing the Dynamic Memory Allocation topic with the tagline 'Memory that keeps on living!'
main_text: This is a section divider slide that introduces the Dynamic Memory Allocation portion of the lecture. The tagline 'Memory that keeps on living!' highlights the core concept: dynamically allocated memory persists beyond the scope of the function that created it, unlike local variables which are destroyed when their function returns.
notes_text: The tagline emphasizes the primary motivation for dynamic allocation: creating memory that outlives the function scope in which it was allocated. This is what distinguishes heap memory from stack memory.

title: A Motivating Task
summary: Presents a motivating coding task: write a function that returns an integer array of size n with values 1 to n, highlighting incomplete return type and body.
main_text: This slide presents a motivating task for dynamic memory allocation. The goal is to write a function ordered_array that takes an integer n and returns an integer array of size n with values 1 to n stored in it. The code skeleton shows a function with a blank return type: _____ ordered_array(int n) { // Your code here ... return ___; }. The main function calls ordered_array and uses the result. The blanks for the return type and return statement are left for students to consider, setting up the discussion of why dynamic allocation is needed to solve this problem.
notes_text: This task is intentionally incomplete to provoke thinking about what return type and mechanism would allow a function to create and return an array. Local arrays would go out of scope, and C++ does not allow returning raw arrays by value, motivating the need for dynamic allocation.

title: 2 Reasons to Use Dynamic Allocation
summary: Identifies two problems with returning arrays from functions: local arrays go out of scope, and variable-length arrays require dynamic sizing.
main_text: This slide identifies two key problems that motivate dynamic allocation. Problem 1: Any array we declare in the ordered_array function will have 'died' (gone out of scope) by the time we return to the calling function. Local variables, including arrays, are destroyed when the function returns. Problem 2: The array would have to be declared with a variable-size (int dat[n]), which is not reliably supported across all C/C++ compilers. The code skeleton from the previous slide is shown again with annotations highlighting both problems. These two issues together demonstrate why dynamic memory allocation is necessary: it allows creating memory that persists beyond function scope and supports runtime-determined sizes.
notes_text: Problem 1 is the primary reason for dynamic allocation. Even if variable-length arrays were universally supported, the scoping issue would remain. Dynamic allocation on the heap solves both problems simultaneously: heap memory persists until explicitly deleted, and the size can be determined at runtime.

title: Dynamic Memory Motivation (2)
summary: Summarizes the primary and secondary reasons for dynamic memory allocation: memory that outlives function scope, and variable-sized arrays at runtime.
main_text: There is ONE primary reason to use dynamic memory allocation and ONE secondary reason. The primary reason is: if we want to have a variable or array STAY ALIVE even AFTER that function ends (i.e. we want to manually control when memory is allocated and DEALLOCATED). The secondary reason is: for variable sized arrays (i.e. we don't know how much memory to allocate until run-time). Two code examples contrast the approaches. The bad approach: int n; // get value of n; int data[n]; // VERY BAD!! This uses a variable-length array which is not portable and considered bad practice. The good approach: int n; // get value of n; int* data = new int[n]; // GOOD! This uses dynamic allocation with the new operator to create an array whose size is determined at runtime.
notes_text: The distinction between primary and secondary reasons is important for exams. The primary reason (memory outliving function scope) is the more fundamental motivation. Variable-sized arrays are a secondary benefit. Students should remember that int data[n] with a runtime variable n is not standard C++ and is forbidden in CS103/104.

title: Dynamic Memory Motivation (1)
summary: Motivates dynamic allocation with a student scores example where array size is unknown until user input, showing why variable-length arrays are bad practice.
main_text: We want to allocate an array for student scores, but we don't know how many students exist until the user inputs it. What size should I use to declare my array? int scores[??]; Doing the following is not supported by all C/C++ compilers and considered bad practice (you may NOT do it in CS103/104): int num; cin >> num; int scores[num]; // Instead, many compilers require the array size to be statically known. Also, recall local variables die when a function returns. What if we need that memory to KEEP LIVING even when our function ends? Both problems are solved with dynamically-allocated (i.e. at run-time) memory.
notes_text: This slide reinforces the motivation from the previous slides with a concrete, relatable example. The student scores scenario is a common real-world case where the size of data is not known at compile time. The explicit prohibition against variable-length arrays in CS103/104 underscores that dynamic allocation is the correct approach.

title: Dynamic Memory Analogy
summary: Uses a public storage rental analogy to explain dynamic memory: rent storage (new), use it via pointer, and return it (delete) to avoid memory leaks.
main_text: Dynamic Memory is 'On-Demand Memory'. The analogy is public storage rentals. Need data to stay alive after the function? Or need a variable-size array? Rent Storage: Use a 'new' statement to allocate the variable or array. The system sets aside memory on the HEAP for you behind the scenes and gives you back a pointer (the start address of that memory for the variable/array). Use Storage: Using the pointer, access the variable or array all you like until you are done with it. It lives INDEFINITELY! Return Storage: You MUST return the memory when you are done with it using a 'delete' statement, or else it cannot be reused/recycled (i.e. a 'memory leak'). Students ask: 'How do I know I'm done with it?' Only you can answer that!
notes_text: The storage rental analogy is very effective for understanding the lifecycle of dynamic memory. Just as you pay rent for a storage unit and must eventually return the key, you allocate heap memory with new and must eventually free it with delete. Forgetting to delete causes memory leaks, where the program gradually consumes more memory without releasing it.

images.description: Photo of orange public storage rental units in a row, illustrating the analogy of renting memory on the heap

title: Dynamic Memory and the Heap
summary: Explains the system stack vs. heap memory layout, showing how the heap is used for dynamic allocation and how stack and heap grow toward each other.
main_text: System stack: Memory for each function that is currently running. It contains local variables, return link (where to return), etc. Heap: Area of memory that can be allocated and de-allocated in chunks during program execution (i.e. dynamically at run-time) based on the needs of the program. Heap and stack grow toward each other. In rare cases of large memory usage, they could collide and cause your program to fail or generate an exception/error. The memory layout diagram shows the following regions from bottom to top: Code (starting at 0x0), Global Data (at 0x10000000), Heap (at 0x18000000, growing upward), unused space in the middle, and Stack (at 0x80000000, growing downward). The top of memory is at 0xffffffff (4GB-1).
notes_text: Understanding the memory layout is fundamental to understanding why dynamic allocation works the way it does. Stack memory is automatically managed (allocated on function entry, freed on function exit). Heap memory is manually managed by the programmer using new and delete. The growing-toward-each-other behavior explains why extremely large allocations can cause stack overflow or heap exhaustion.

images.description: Vertical memory layout diagram showing Code at bottom (0x0), Global Data (0x10000000), Heap growing upward (0x18000000), empty space, and Stack growing downward (0x80000000), with arrows showing growth directions

title: C (Pre-C++) Dynamic Allocation
summary: Describes C-style dynamic allocation using malloc and free functions, noting that the course will use only C++ new/delete methods.
main_text: C-style dynamic allocation uses two functions from stdlib.h. void* malloc(int num_bytes) function: Allocates the number of bytes requested and returns a pointer to the block of memory. free(void * ptr) function: Given the pointer to the (starting location of the) block of memory, free returns it to the system for re-use by subsequent malloc calls. This slide is for completeness. We will only use the C++ methods on the next slide in this class!
notes_text: While malloc and free are the C approach to dynamic memory management, CS103 focuses exclusively on the C++ new and delete operators. However, understanding malloc/free is valuable because many legacy codebases and system-level code still use them. The key difference is that new/delete are type-aware and call constructors/destructors, while malloc/free work with raw bytes.

title: C++ new Operator
summary: Explains the C++ new operator for heap allocation, showing syntax for single values and arrays, and the rule that new T always returns T*.
main_text: The new operator allocates memory from the heap. It replaced C's malloc() function. new should be followed with the type of the variable (and, if allocating an array, the size). Examples: double *dptr = new double; allocates 1 double. int *scores = new int[n]; allocates an n-integer array. new T or new T[n] returns a pointer of type T*. If you ask for a new int, you get an int* in return. If you ask for a new array (new int[n]), you still get an int* in return. Hard and Fast Rule of Dynamic Allocation: If you dynamically allocate a single type T or even a T array, you will ALWAYS get back a pointer of type T*. new T; yields a type T*. new T[n]; yields a type T*. The memory layout diagram shows dptr and scores as pointers on the stack pointing to their respective allocations on the heap.
notes_text: The 'Hard and Fast Rule' is critical for exams and practical coding: new always returns a pointer of the same base type, regardless of whether you allocated a single element or an array. This connects back to slide 2's discussion about pointer ambiguity - the type system alone cannot tell you if the pointer references one element or many.

images.description: Memory layout diagram showing stack with dptr (0x18097520) and scores (0x18004200) pointers pointing to their respective heap allocations, with Code, Global Data, Heap, and Stack regions labeled

title: C++ delete Operator
summary: Explains the C++ delete operator for deallocating heap memory, distinguishing delete for single values and delete[] for arrays.
main_text: Given these allocations: double *dptr = new double; (allocates 1 double) and int *scores = new int[n]; Use the data via the pointers. When you are done, you must call delete to return the memory to the heap. delete replaces C's free() function. It is followed by the pointer to the data you want to de-allocate: delete dptr; Use delete [] for arrays: delete [] scores; Important clarification: delete dptr; DOES NOT delete dptr, but what dptr points at (i.e. the memory on the heap). The memory layout diagram shows the heap allocations being marked with X symbols after delete is called, indicating the memory is returned to the heap for reuse.
notes_text: The distinction between delete and delete[] is critical. Using delete on memory allocated with new[] (or vice versa) causes undefined behavior. The clarification that delete frees the heap memory, not the pointer variable itself, is a common source of confusion. After delete, the pointer still exists on the stack but now points to freed memory (a dangling pointer).

images.description: Memory layout diagram showing stack pointers dptr and scores with their heap allocations crossed out (X marks) after delete, illustrating memory being returned to the heap

title: Example of Variable Size Array with Dynamic Allocation
summary: Complete code example showing dynamic allocation of a variable-sized array for student scores, with memory diagram showing heap and stack layout.
main_text: This example demonstrates the secondary reason for dynamic allocation: variable-sized arrays. The code: int main(int argc, char *argv[]) { int num; cout << "How many students?" << endl; cin >> num; int *scores = new int[num]; // can now access scores[0..num-1] for(int i=0; i < num; i++){ cin >> scores[i]; } // Do more with scores // free up scores delete [] scores; return 0; }. The memory diagram shows the layout: Code at bottom, Globals above, then Heap containing the dynamically allocated array (int[0] through int[num-1] starting at address 20bc0), and Stack at top containing the int* scores pointer (holding value 20bc0, the address of the heap array). Recall the two reasons to use dynamic allocation: Secondary reason: Variable size array (seen in this example). Primary reason: Allocate memory that should not go out of scope at the end of the function (seen in next example).
notes_text: This is a practical, complete example students can compile and run. Note the full lifecycle: allocate with new int[num], use the array with bracket notation scores[i], and free with delete [] scores. The memory diagram helps visualize how the pointer on the stack references data on the heap.

images.description: Memory layout diagram showing Code, Globals, Heap with array elements int[0] through int[num-1] at addresses 20bc0-20bc8+, and Stack with int* scores pointer holding address 20bc0

title: Example of Variable Size Array with Dynamic Allocation (Cross-Function)
summary: Shows dynamic allocation across functions: getArray allocates on the heap and returns the pointer, main uses and deletes it.
main_text: This example demonstrates the primary reason for dynamic allocation: memory that outlives function scope. The code shows two functions: int* getArray(int n) { int *dat = new int[n]; // or int dat[n]; // can now access scores[0..n-1] for(int i=0; i < n; i++){ cin >> dat[i]; } return dat; }. int main(int argc, char *argv[]) { int num, sum = 0; cout << "How many students?" << endl; cin >> num; int* scores = getArray(num); for(int i=0; i < num; i++) { sum += scores[i]; } delete [] scores; // free up scores return 0; }. The memory diagram shows getArray's stack frame with int* dat pointing to heap memory at 20bc0, and main's stack frame with int* scores also holding 20bc0. When getArray returns, dat is destroyed but the heap memory survives. main receives the pointer and is responsible for deleting it.
notes_text: This is the key example for understanding the primary motivation. The heap array allocated in getArray survives after getArray returns because heap memory is not tied to function scope. The caller (main) receives the pointer and assumes ownership, including the responsibility to delete the memory. This ownership transfer pattern is fundamental in C++ programming.

images.description: Memory layout diagram showing getArray's stack frame with int* dat and main's stack frame with int* scores, both pointing to the same heap array at address 20bc0

title: Fill in the Blanks - Pointer Types (Exercise)
summary: Exercise slide asking students to determine the correct pointer type for various new expressions, with blanks to fill in.
main_text: This exercise asks students to fill in the correct pointer type declaration for each dynamic allocation statement. The expressions are: _______ data = new int; _______ data = new char; _______ data = new char[100]; _______ data = new double[20]; _______ data = new string; _______ data = new char*[10]; Students must apply the Hard and Fast Rule: new T always returns T*, and new T[n] also returns T*. This tests understanding that the pointer type matches the base type being allocated, regardless of whether a single element or array is created.
notes_text: This is a self-assessment exercise. Students should pause and attempt to fill in each blank before proceeding to the answer slide. The key insight is that new T and new T[n] both yield T*. The last case (new char*[10]) is trickier because the base type is char*, so the result is char**.

title: Fill in the Blanks - Pointer Types (Answers)
summary: Answer slide revealing the correct pointer types: int*, char*, char*, double*, string*, and char** for the respective new expressions.
main_text: The answers to the fill-in-the-blanks exercise are: int* data = new int; (new int yields int*). char* data = new char; (new char yields char*). char* data = new char[100]; (new char[100] still yields char*). double* data = new double[20]; (new double[20] yields double*). string* data = new string; (new string yields string*). char** data = new char*[10]; (new char*[10] yields char**, because the base type is char*, and adding the pointer from new gives char**). This confirms the Hard and Fast Rule: new T or new T[n] always returns T*.
notes_text: The char** case is particularly important. When allocating an array of char* (pointers to characters, often used for arrays of C-strings), the result is a pointer to a pointer, or char**. This pattern appears frequently when working with 2D arrays or arrays of strings in C-style code.

title: Correct Usage of Pointers
summary: Demonstrates correct pointer usage with an area computation example comparing return-by-value (area1) and pass-by-pointer (area2) approaches.
main_text: Commonly functions will take some inputs and produce some outputs. We'll use a simple 'area' function for now even though we can easily compute this without a function. We could use the return value but let's practice with pointers and say mul() must return void. Can use a pointer to have a function modify the variable of another. The code shows: int area1(int w, int h) { return w * h; } which returns by value. void area2(int w, int h, int* a) { *a = w * h; } which uses a pointer parameter to write the result into the caller's variable. In main: int wid = 8, ht = 5, a; area2(wid, len, &a); cout << "Ans. is " << a << endl; The stack diagram shows two frames: main with wid=8, ht=5, a (which gets overwritten with 40), and area with w=8, h=5, out=0x7bf8 (pointing to main's a variable). The return link shows where execution returns after area finishes.
notes_text: This slide reviews pass-by-pointer, which was covered earlier in the course. The stack diagram is essential for understanding how area2's pointer parameter 'out' holds the address of main's variable 'a', allowing area2 to modify a's value. This is Reason 1 for using pointers from slide 3.

images.description: Stack diagram showing two frames: area (w=8, h=5, out=0x7bf8, return link) and main (wid=8, ht=5, a with value 40 written via pointer, return link), with out pointing to main's a variable

title: Pointer Mistake - Returning Pointer to Local Variable (Setup)
summary: Introduces a critical pointer mistake: returning the address of a local variable from a function, which creates a dangling pointer.
main_text: Never return a pointer to a local variable. The code shows a flawed area3 function: int* area3(int w, int l) { int ans; ans = w * l; return &ans; // X - THIS IS WRONG }. In main: int wid = 8, len = 5, *a; a = area3(wid, len); cout << *a << endl; The stack diagram shows: when area3 is running, its frame contains ans=0x93c (with computed value), w=8, l=5, and a return link. main's frame contains wid=8, len=5, a=-73249515 (garbage). The pointer 'a' in main receives the address of area3's local variable 'ans', but once area3 returns, that stack memory is reclaimed and the pointer becomes dangling.
notes_text: This is one of the most common and dangerous pointer mistakes. The address &ans is valid only while area3 is executing. Once area3 returns, its stack frame is deallocated, and any pointer to that memory becomes a dangling pointer. Dereferencing a dangling pointer causes undefined behavior - it might appear to work sometimes, making the bug hard to detect.

images.description: Stack diagram showing area3 frame with ans, w, l, return link, and main frame with wid, len, a holding garbage value, illustrating that area3's local variable ans will be destroyed on return

title: Pointer Mistake - Dangling Pointer After Return
summary: Shows what happens after the function returns: the pointer points to dead stack memory, creating a dangling pointer that leads to corruption.
main_text: Never return a pointer to a local variable. Pointer will now point to dead memory and the value it was pointing at will be soon corrupted/overwritten. We call this a dangling pointer (i.e. a pointer to bad or dead memory). The code is the same flawed area3 function: int* area3(int, int); void print(int); int main() { int wid = 8, len = 5, *a; a = area3(wid, len); cout << *a << endl; }. int* area(int w, int l) { int ans; ans = w * l; return &ans; // X - WRONG }. The stack diagram now shows only main's frame (area3 has returned): wid=8, len=5, a=0xbe0. An arrow from a points upward to where area3's stack frame used to be, which is now empty/dead memory. The heap area is also shown as empty. This illustrates that the pointer a now references memory that no longer belongs to any active function.
notes_text: After area3 returns, its stack frame is gone. The pointer 'a' in main still holds the old address (0xbe0) where ans used to live, but that memory is now available for reuse by any future function call. Reading from *a gives unpredictable results, and writing to *a could corrupt another function's data. This is why the correct approach is to use dynamic allocation (new) so the data lives on the heap.

images.description: Stack and heap diagram showing main's frame with pointer 'a' pointing to empty space above the stack where area3's frame used to exist, illustrating the dangling pointer problem after function return

title: Dynamic Allocation - Correct Solution with new
summary: Shows the correct approach: using new int to allocate on the heap so the value survives after the function returns, with proper delete in main.
main_text: Dynamic Allocation properties: Lives on the heap. Doesn't have a name, only pointer/address to it. Lives until you 'delete' it. Doesn't die at end of function (though pointer to it may). You must keep at least 1 pointer to a dynamic memory allocation at all times until it is deleted. The corrected code: int* area3(int w, int l) { int* ans = new int; *ans = w * l; return ans; }. int main() { int wid = 8, len = 5, *a; a = area3(wid, len); cout << *a << endl; // 40 delete a; return 0; }. The stack/heap diagram shows: area3's frame has ans=0x93c (a pointer to heap), w=8, l=5. The heap contains value 40 at address 0x93c. main's frame has wid=8, len=5, a=0x93c. After area3 returns, main's pointer a still validly points to the heap value 40. The delete annotation shows where heap memory is freed.
notes_text: This is the correct version of the area3 function. By allocating with new int on the heap, the integer value survives after area3 returns. The pointer ans in area3 dies (it's a local variable), but its value (the heap address) is returned to main and stored in a. main is then responsible for calling delete a to free the heap memory. This is the fundamental pattern of dynamic allocation.

images.description: Stack and heap diagram showing area3 frame with pointer ans=0x93c on stack pointing to heap value 40 at address 0x93c, and main frame with pointer a=0x93c also pointing to same heap location, with delete annotation

title: Dynamic Allocation - Memory Leak Example
summary: Demonstrates a memory leak: commenting out delete leaves heap memory allocated but inaccessible, wasting resources indefinitely.
main_text: Dynamic Allocation properties (repeated): Lives on the heap. Doesn't have a name, only pointer/address to it. Lives until you 'delete' it. Doesn't die at end of function (though pointer to it may). You should remember to delete the memory you allocated. The code shows the memory leak scenario: int main() { int wid = 8, len = 5, *a; a = area3(wid, len); cout << *a << endl; // 40 // delete a; <-- commented out! return 0; }. int* area3(int w, int l) { int* ans = new int; *ans = w * l; return ans; }. The stack/heap diagram shows main's frame with wid=8, len=5, a=0x93c pointing to heap value 40 at 0x93c. A label 'Memory Leak!' appears next to the heap allocation, indicating that the memory at 0x93c will never be freed because delete was commented out.
notes_text: Memory leaks are a common bug in C++ programs. In this small example the leak is trivial because the program is about to exit anyway. However, in long-running programs (servers, games, embedded systems), memory leaks accumulate over time and can eventually exhaust available memory, causing crashes. Tools like Valgrind can detect memory leaks.

images.description: Stack and heap diagram showing main frame with pointer a pointing to heap value 40, with 'Memory Leak!' label indicating the heap memory is never freed

title: Dynamic Allocation - Failure to Save Pointer (Crash)
summary: Shows a crash scenario where the returned pointer from area3 is never saved, causing both a memory leak and a crash when dereferencing an invalid pointer.
main_text: Dynamic Allocation properties (repeated): Lives on the heap. Doesn't have a name, only pointer/address to it. Lives until you 'delete' it. Doesn't die at end of function (though pointer to it may). This code fails to save a pointer to the new int once area() finishes. The buggy code: int main() { int wid = 8, len = 5, *a; area3(wid, len); // return value NOT saved! cout << *a << endl; // crash return 0; }. int* area3(int w, int l) { int* ans = new int; *ans = w * l; return ans; }. The stack/heap diagram shows: area3's frame has ans=0x93c pointing to heap value 40. But in main, a=-73249515 (uninitialized garbage). The heap allocation at 0x93c is labeled 'MEMORY LEAK - No one saved a pointer to this data'. The pointer a in main points to an invalid address, labeled 'CRASH'. Two bugs occur simultaneously: a memory leak (heap memory with no pointer to it) and a crash (dereferencing uninitialized pointer a).
notes_text: This example combines two bugs: (1) the return value of area3 is discarded, so the heap memory becomes unreachable (memory leak), and (2) the uninitialized pointer a in main contains garbage, so dereferencing it with *a causes a segmentation fault or crash. Always save the return value of functions that allocate memory.

images.description: Stack and heap diagram showing area3 frame with ans pointing to heap value 40 (labeled MEMORY LEAK), and main frame with uninitialized pointer a pointing to invalid address (labeled CRASH)

title: Exercises
summary: Closing slide directing students to practice exercises related to dynamic memory allocation concepts covered in this unit.
main_text: This is the closing slide for Unit 2c, directing students to exercises that reinforce the concepts covered in this lecture. Students should practice writing code that uses new and delete, identifying memory leaks, avoiding dangling pointers, and determining correct pointer types for dynamic allocations.
notes_text: Students should review all the examples from this unit and practice tracing through code with stack and heap diagrams. Key skills to practice include: allocating and freeing memory, returning dynamically allocated memory from functions, identifying bugs like memory leaks and dangling pointers, and filling in correct pointer types.
